name: Supplementary Relative

1.definition: Adds a separate predication about a referent or a larger anchor.

examples.form: Jo visited Bath, [which she had never seen before].

projection.target: The clause can add information about an already identified referent. Substituting bare that-relative syntax generally fails in the same supplementary reading.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: A which clause that adds extra information
curious.summary: A which clause after a name can add a separate piece of information about it.
curious.body: In Jo visited Bath, which she had never seen before, the which clause adds a second statement. It tells us something more about Bath, a place already identified. It doesn't help us work out which place is meant. A which clause can also add information about a larger anchor than a single noun. This dictionary notes that swapping in a bare that-relative generally fails to give the same added-information reading. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional and rests on one constructed illustration.

examples.text: Jo visited Bath, [which she had never seen before].

curious.try: Add a which clause after the name of a place you know, and say what extra information it gives.

teacher.summary: Helps explain which clauses that add information about an already identified referent, set off by commas.
teacher.explain: The pattern is an anchor followed by a supplementary wh-relative clause. It adds a separate predication about a referent or a larger anchor: in Jo visited Bath, which she had never seen before, the clause adds information about Bath, an already identified referent. Substituting bare that-relative syntax generally fails in the same supplementary reading. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional and has one constructed illustration. It lists the relative word as a part of this pattern.
teacher.terms: Traditional grammar sometimes calls this a non-restrictive relative clause. CGEL: supplementary relative clause.

examples.text: Jo visited Bath, [which she had never seen before].

watch_for: A learner might read the which clause as helping to pick out which place is meant, when it adds information about a place already identified.
A learner might swap in that for which and expect the same added-information reading.
teacher.activity: Students write a sentence naming a place, then add a which clause with extra information about it. A partner explains what the clause adds and whether it helps identify the place.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Supplementary Relative." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/supplementary-relative-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).
